title: Do carrots give you night vision?
transcript: Somebody told you to eat your carrots so you can see in the dark. Ever wonder who started that?
So do carrots really give you night vision?
Back to Britain, nineteen forty. Enemy bombers came at night, so the whole country switched off its lights.
A pilot named John Cunningham kept finding bombers in the dark. They nicknamed him Cat's Eyes, and newspapers were told that pilots like him ate lots of carrots.

The real secret was radar, a new machine in his plane that found what his eyes couldn't. Cunningham later said the nickname was made up to hide it. Historians still argue about whether the enemy fell for it.
Britain also had piles of carrots, so the government made a cartoon called Doctor Carrot. Posters said carrots help you see in the blackout.
Here's the truth. Carrots have vitamin A, and your eyes need it to see in dim light. If you're low on it, carrots help. If you get enough, more carrots won't give you super night vision.
One more legend. People say Dutch farmers made carrots orange to honor their prince, William of Orange. Carrot historians say there's no proof.
The first farmed carrots, in Central Asia, were purple and yellow. Orange ones showed up in Europe around five hundred years ago. The royal fan club came later.
Try this: a rainbow carrot taste test. Purple, yellow, white, orange. Can you tell them apart with your eyes closed?
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- **Blackouts, A.I. radar, Cunningham "Cat's Eyes", newspapers told pilots ate carrots, Doctor Carrot, Dig for Victory, 100,000-ton carrot surplus by 1942, "help you see in the blackout" posters, Stolarczyk: "I have no evidence they fell for it"** · Smithsonian Magazine, "A WWII Propaganda Campaign Popularized the Myth That Carrots Help You See in the Dark" (draws on the World Carrot Museum, Imperial War Museums images and the U.K. National Archives): https://www.smithsonianmag.com/arts-culture/a-wwii-propaganda-campaign-popularized-the-myth-that-carrots-help-you-see-in-the-dark-28812484/
- **Cunningham's own words: "I was given the nickname 'Cat's Eyes' by the Air Ministry to cover up the fact that we were flying aircraft with radar"; Lord Woolton (Minister of Food) promoting carrots; AI (Airborne Interception) radar** · Air & Space / Smithsonian, "Cat's Eyes": https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history-of-flight/cats-eyes-72622832/
- **Dispute over who the story was aimed at: RAF Museum's Bryan Legate says the Air Ministry "never set out to use it to fool the Germans"; vitamin A matters for low-light vision (Emily Chew, National Eye Institute); extra carrots don't improve vision in people who already get enough** · Scientific American, "Fact or Fiction?: Carrots Improve Your Vision": https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-carrots-improve-your-vision/ · also Science Norway (RAF Museum quote): https://www.sciencenorway.no/culture-food-and-health-war/where-the-carrot-myth-comes-from/2665915
- **First cultivated carrots were purple or yellow; domestication in the Afghanistan region** · Soufflet-Freslon et al., *PLoS One* 2013, 8(8): e70801: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3733727
- **Domesticated carrot originated in Central Asia (genetics + historical documents)** · Iorizzo et al., *American Journal of Botany* 2013, 100(5): 930-938: https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/id/eprint/54258
- **Earliest domesticated carrots in Central Asia were purple and yellow; "orange roots appeared in Spain and Germany in the 16th century"** · Ellison et al. (incl. Iorizzo, Simon), *Genetics* 2018, 210(4): 1497-1508: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/6283172/
- **House of Orange story lacks evidence; Stolarczyk (World Carrot Museum): "the orange carrot came first, the Royal family dedication second"; Philipp Simon dismisses the tribute claim** · DutchNews.nl, 2016: https://www.dutchnews.nl/2016/05/90146-2
notesMd:
- **Radar cover story.** Cunningham himself said the "Cat's Eyes" nickname was meant to hide radar, and the government told
  newspapers the pilots ate carrots. Whether the goal was to fool *Germany* is disputed (the RAF Museum curator says no;
  others say it was mostly to sell surplus carrots to the British public). The narration says "Historians still argue about
  whether the enemy fell for it" and never claims the Germans were fooled. The "enemy pilot nibbling a carrot" gag ends on a
  "?" to keep it a question; the tales of Luftwaffe pilots eating carrots are apocryphal, so they are not narrated.
- **"First" radar kill.** Smithsonian says Cunningham was the first British pilot to shoot down a plane with A.I. radar; another
  account calls it "one of the first". The narration avoids "first".
- **Vitamin A.** Carrots supply beta carotene that the body turns into vitamin A; deficiency causes night blindness. The line
  "If you're low on it, carrots help" is a simplification of that. No claim of better-than-normal vision.
- **Orange carrots.** Dates vary by source (16th century in Spain/Germany per *Genetics* 2018; 1600s per *PLoS One* 2013;
  Dutch paintings in the early 1600s). The narration says "around five hundred years ago" in "Europe", which fits the
  16th-century date, and does not credit the Dutch with inventing orange. The House of Orange link is presented as a legend
  with "no proof"; the royal association came later. Some Dutch sources still repeat the tribute story, so it is framed as
  what "people say".

title: Why does cilantro taste like soap?
transcript: You take a big bite of taco, and suddenly it tastes like you licked a bar of soap.
So why does cilantro taste like soap to some people, and like fresh, lemony leaves to everyone else?
Cilantro is full of smelly chemicals called aldehydes. And guess what soap makers often use to make soap smell nice? Aldehydes.
Scientists think the difference is in your nose, not your tongue.
In twenty twelve, scientists asked about fourteen thousand six hundred people one question: does fresh cilantro taste like soap to you? Almost two thousand said yes. That's about one in seven.

The soap tasters were more likely to have one tiny spelling change in their DNA, right next to a family of smell sensor genes. One of those sensors, called O R six A two, grabs onto cilantro's smells.
But genes aren't the whole story. The same team found that the genes they could measure explained only a small part of it.
It also changes around the world. In a Toronto study, about one in five East Asian young adults disliked cilantro. Among Middle Eastern young adults, it was about three in a hundred.
Fun fact: one of cilantro's smells, called decanal, is also made by oranges.
Try this: pass some cilantro around the table and sniff. Who smells salad, and who smells soap? Nobody's wrong.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- **GWAS: 14,604 European-ancestry 23andMe participants asked "Does fresh cilantro taste like soap to you?"; SNP rs72921001 in an olfactory receptor gene cluster on chromosome 11 including OR6A2, which binds several cilantro aldehydes; heritability tagged by common SNPs about 0.087 (a lower bound); cilantro aldehydes include decanal and (E)-2-decenal, the latter described as soapy** · Eriksson et al., "A genetic variant near olfactory receptor genes influences cilantro preference", *Flavour* 2012, 1:22: https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.2096 · PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1209.2096
- **1,994 of the 14,604 said cilantro tasted like soap (about 13.7%, roughly one in seven); soaps are often scented with aldehydes; scientists suspect differences in smell, not taste; decanal is also made by oranges** · American Chemical Society, ChemMatters, "Cilantro: Delicious or Disgusting?": https://www.acs.org/education/chemmatters/articles/cilantro-delicious-or-disgusting.html
- **Dislike prevalence by group in 1,639 Toronto adults aged 20-29: East Asian 21%, Caucasian 17%, African 14%, South Asian 7%, Hispanic 4%, Middle Eastern 3%** · Mauer & El-Sohemy, "Prevalence of cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) disliking among different ethnocultural groups", *Flavour* 2012, 1:8: https://flavourjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/2044-7248-1-8
notesMd:
- **"One in seven."** 1,994 / 14,604 = 13.7% in one self-selected group of 23andMe customers of European ancestry. It is not a
  world figure, so the narration ties it to "fourteen thousand six hundred people", not "everyone". Popular articles quote
  anything from 4% to 21%; we only use the two studies above.
- **The gene.** It's an association near a *cluster* of smell receptor genes; OR6A2 is the authors' best candidate, not proven.
  The narration says "more likely to have" and "right next to a family of smell sensor genes", and "grabs onto cilantro's
  smells" matches the paper's "high binding specificity for several of the aldehydes".
- **Genes are a small part.** The paper's measured heritability was low (0.087, a lower bound). The narration says "the genes
  they could measure explained only a small part of it" rather than giving a percentage.
- **Smell, not taste.** ACS says scientists *suspect* smell explains it; narration says "Scientists think".
- **Cut on purpose.** The popular tip that crushing or chopping cilantro makes it less soapy (Harold McGee, NYT 2010, citing
  Japanese research) could only be checked through secondary summaries, so it is left out. The 23andMe ancestry percentages
  from the company blog were also left out in favor of the peer-reviewed Toronto numbers.

title: What is brain freeze, really?
transcript: You slurp a giant milkshake way too fast. And then, ouch. A sharp pain, right behind your forehead.
So what is brain freeze? Is your brain actually freezing?
Doctors call it sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia. Try saying that with a mouth full of ice cream. Everybody else just says brain freeze.
Here's the myth buster: your brain is not freezing. When something icy touches the roof of your mouth, the blood vessels in your head react to the sudden cold.
In twenty twelve, scientists had thirteen grown-ups sip ice water through a straw pressed against the roof of their mouth, while a machine watched blood flow in their brains.
When the pain hit, a big blood vessel near the front of the brain suddenly widened and blood rushed in. When it narrowed again, the pain faded.
Scientists think it may be your body rushing in warm blood to protect your brain. They're still working out exactly why it hurts.

And one brain freeze study was led by a kid. A thirteen year old in Canada had a hundred forty-five middle schoolers eat ice cream. The fast eaters got brain freeze about twice as often as the slow eaters.
How to stop it: press your tongue or your thumb against the roof of your mouth, or sip something that isn't cold. It usually goes away in seconds, and it isn't harmful.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- **Medical name "sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia"; blood vessels in the head react to extreme cold; lasts a few seconds to two minutes; not serious; stop by drinking a warm or room-temperature liquid or pressing tongue or thumb against the roof of the mouth** · Cleveland Clinic, "Brain Freeze": https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/21478-brain-freeze
- **2012 study: 13 healthy adults sipped ice water through a straw against the upper palate; transcranial Doppler measured brain blood flow; the anterior cerebral artery dilated rapidly as pain began and constricted as it faded; possible self-protection of the brain; led by Jorge Serrador (Harvard Medical School / VA New Jersey), presented at Experimental Biology 2012** · ScienceDaily (American Physiological Society release): https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/04/120422231742.htm
- **Kid-led trial: 145 students at Dalewood Middle School, Hamilton, Ontario; 100 ml ice cream in under 5 s vs over 30 s; headache in 27% (20/73) vs 13% (9/72); 59% of headaches lasted under 10 s; funded by "an unrestricted grant from mum and dad"** · Kaczorowski M, Kaczorowski J, "Ice cream evoked headaches (ICE-H) study", *BMJ* 2002;325:1445: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC139031
- **Maya Kaczorowski was 13** · CBS News: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/brain-freeze/
notesMd:
- **Mechanism is not settled.** The 2012 study was small (13 adults), first presented as a conference abstract, and shows the
  artery change *goes with* the pain. Why it hurts (pressure in the skull, a nerve in the palate) is still debated. The
  narration says "Scientists think it may be" and "They're still working out exactly why it hurts".
- **"Near the front of the brain"** is a kid-friendly stand-in for the anterior cerebral artery.
- **"About twice as often."** 27% vs 13% (relative risk 2.2, wide confidence interval 1.03 to 4.94). The narration says
  "about twice as often", which matches. "Led by a kid" is fair: Maya Kaczorowski was first author and ran it as a science
  project; her father, a McMaster University researcher, was co-author.
- **The name.** Cleveland Clinic gives "sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia" as the scientific term; the narration only says
  doctors call it that, without claiming that ganglion is the cause.

title: Are bananas radioactive?
transcript: You pack a banana in your lunch. Guess what? It's a tiny bit radioactive.
Wait. Radioactive? Should you be worried?
Bananas have lots of potassium, and your body needs potassium. But a teeny fraction of all potassium is a radioactive kind, called potassium forty.
It's not just in bananas. All plants and animals have a little potassium forty. That includes you.
Scientists even use a joke unit for tiny amounts of radiation: the banana equivalent dose. One banana gives you about zero point one microsieverts.
That is tiny. You'd have to eat about one hundred bananas to match the radiation people in the United States get from nature every single day.
And here's the twist. Bananas don't pile up radiation inside you. Your body keeps its potassium level steady, so the extra goes out in your pee, almost right away.
Bananas aren't even the champions. Carrots and potatoes have almost as much potassium forty. Lima beans have more. And Brazil nuts have more still, plus some radium.
Fun fact to share at lunch: you are a little bit radioactive too, and that's totally normal.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- **A small fraction of all potassium is radioactive; one banana gives about 0.01 millirem (0.1 microsieverts); about 100 bananas equal the dose a person in the United States gets each day from natural environmental sources; these foods "do not pose a radiation risk"** · U.S. EPA RadTown, "Natural Radioactivity in Food": https://www.epa.gov/radtown/natural-radioactivity-food
- **"All organic matter (both plant and animal) contains some small amount of radiation from radioactive potassium-40"; K-40 per kg: bananas 3,520 pCi, carrots 3,400, white potatoes 3,400, raw lima beans 4,640, Brazil nuts 5,600 (plus 1,000-7,000 pCi/kg radium-226); average internal dose from food and water about 30 millirem per year** · U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, "Doses in Our Daily Lives": https://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/radiation/around-us/doses-daily-lives.html
- **Banana equivalent dose is a "fake unit" of about 0.1 microsievert; excess potassium is excreted in urine almost immediately, so eating bananas has practically no effect on the dose you actually receive** · University of Groningen, Radiation Protection A-Z, "Banana equivalent dose": https://www.rug.nl/education/courses/other-education/radiation-protection/a-z/a-z-data/banana-equivalent-dose
notesMd:
- **0.1 microsievert is a rounded, informal number.** Calculations range about 0.08-0.1 µSv depending on the dose
  coefficient used; EPA states 0.1. The narration says "about".
- **"About one hundred bananas a day of nature"** is EPA's comparison for the U.S. average, so the narration says "people in the
  United States".
- **The twist is the honest core.** Because the body holds potassium steady (homeostasis), a banana barely changes your actual
  internal dose; the "banana dose" is a comparison yardstick, which the narration calls "a joke unit".
- **"Almost right away"** follows the Groningen wording ("bijna onmiddellijk"). It is a simplification of the kidneys
  restoring balance over hours.
- **Brazil nuts.** NRC lists more K-40 per kg and far more radium than bananas. "Some radium" makes no safety claim either way.
- **Cut on purpose.** The popular story that banana shipments set off port radiation detectors is disputed (other sources say
  ceramics and clay litter, not bananas, are the usual triggers), so it is left out.

title: Why do kids love sweet?
transcript: You were born with a sweet tooth, before you had a single tooth.
So why do kids love sweet so much more than grown-ups?
Put a drop of something sweet on a newborn baby's tongue, and their little face relaxes. Babies come out liking sweet. It helps draw them to milk.
Scientists even have a name for your perfect amount of sweet. It's called your bliss point. And kids have a higher bliss point than grown-ups.

In a twenty twenty study, kids, teens, and grown-ups tasted cups of sugar water. Grown-ups liked about eight sugar cubes in a glass of water, about as sweet as a cola. Kids and teens liked it fifty percent sweeter, about twelve sugar cubes.
Why? One idea is that growing bodies need lots of energy, and sweet tastes mean energy.

Then something changes. In a study of eleven to fifteen year olds, teens whose bones were growing less tended to like sugar less. By the late teen years, most sweet tooths settle down to grown-up levels.
So a kid's sweet tooth isn't about having no willpower. A lot of it is biology. And what kids taste early on can shape what they like later.
Try this: a blueberry taste test. In one study, kids were better than their moms at telling which blueberries were sweeter.
Wonderade is made with real fruit, with three grams of sugar and zero grams added. Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- **Children are born preferring sweet, which attracts them to mother's milk; a sweet solution in the mouth relaxes an infant's face and calms crying newborns; children prefer higher sweetness than adults; an age-related "bliss point"; preference declines to adult levels in middle to late adolescence, possibly related to the end of growth; heightened preference may relate to a growing child's need for calories; infants fed sugar water later preferred sweeter solutions** · Mennella & Bobowski, "The sweetness and bitterness of childhood: Insights from basic research on taste preferences", *Physiology & Behavior* 2015;152:502-507 (Monell Chemical Senses Center): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4654709/
- **Sensory experiences beginning early in life shape preferences** · Mennella, "Ontogeny of taste preferences: basic biology and implications for health", *Am J Clin Nutr* 2014: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3927698 · and Ventura & Mennella, "Innate and learned preferences for sweet taste during childhood", 2011: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21508837/
- **2020 study (Petty, Salame, Mennella, Pepino; *Nutrients*): 108 children, 172 adolescents, 205 adults aged 7-67; adults preferred about cola-level sweetness, about 8 sugar cubes in an 8-ounce glass of water; children and adolescents preferred about 50% more, about 12 cubes** · University of Illinois news release: https://news.illinois.edu/sweet-taste-perception-changes-as-children-develop/
- **143 children aged 11-15; low-sugar-preference group had lower levels of a bone-growth marker; "the change in sugar preference from high to low during adolescence appears to be associated with the cessation of growth"** · Coldwell, Oswald & Reed, "A marker of growth differs between adolescents with high versus low sugar preference", *Physiology & Behavior* 2009: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2764307/
- **Blueberry study: 49 children and their mothers at Monell; children more sensitive to small differences in blueberry sweetness and a higher fructose bliss point; Mennella: kids' "perfect amount of sweetness in a food is higher for them than adults"** · UF/IFAS news, 2017: https://blogs.ifas.ufl.edu/news/2017/06/27/achieving-bliss-children-adults-differ-perceive-sweetness-fruits/
notesMd:
- **"Kids and teens" fifty percent sweeter.** The 2020 study grouped children and adolescents together for this result; the
  narration keeps both.
- **Growth link is an association.** Coldwell 2009 found a lower bone-growth marker in the low-preference teens; the reason is
  not proven. The narration says "tended to", and the energy idea is "One idea". "Late teen years" follows Mennella's
  "middle to late adolescence".
- **"Not willpower, biology."** Our framing, not a quoted myth. It says "a lot of it is biology" (not all of it), and the next
  sentence notes that early tastes shape later likes, so it doesn't sound like destiny.
- **"It helps draw them to milk."** Mennella & Bobowski say sweet preference attracts infants to mother's milk; the line says
  "milk" to stay inclusive of formula-fed families without adding a claim.
- **Blueberries.** The study compared children with their mothers ("kids were better than their moms"), so the line says moms,
  not "grown-ups".
- **Cut on purpose.** The "bliss point" term is also associated with food-industry research (Howard Moskowitz); that history
  wasn't verified here and isn't needed.

title: The boy who cracked vanilla
transcript: You lick vanilla ice cream. Mmm. That flavor started out as a flower.
So why is real vanilla so expensive?
Vanilla is an orchid. The vanilla bean is the pod that grows after its flower gets pollinated.
Vanilla comes from Mexico, where bees carry the pollen. When people planted it on islands far away, the vines made flowers, but hardly any beans.
Then, in eighteen forty-one, on an island called Réunion, a twelve-year-old boy named Edmond figured it out. Edmond was enslaved. That means he was forced to work and was not free.
He used a thin little stick to lift a tiny flap inside the flower, then pressed the two parts together with his thumb. Pollen in place. Bean on the way.

Here's the tricky part. A grown-up botanist later said Edmond copied him. Historians who studied the old letters say no, Edmond worked it out himself. A Belgian professor had done it in a lab years before, but Edmond's quick, simple way is the one farmers use.

Farmers still do it by hand today, one flower at a time. Each flower is ready for only a few hours. Then the pods grow for about eight months and get cured for months more. That's why real vanilla costs so much.
Edmond became free in eighteen forty-eight, when France ended slavery in its colonies. He was never paid for his discovery.
So next time you taste vanilla, remember Edmond.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- Edmond, born 1829 on Bourbon (now Réunion), enslaved, discovered hand-pollination in 1841 aged 12; Bellier-Beaumont's
  1861 letter; Richard's competing claim and Arditti et al. (2009) concluding Edmond worked it out himself; freed
  around the April 1848 abolition and given the surname Albius; died at 51 without a stipend; *Vanilla planifolia*
  native to Mexico, pollinated there by *Eulaema* bees. Linnean Society: https://linnean.org/news/2019/10/16/edmond-albius
- Twelve years old in 1841; enslaved on Réunion; used a small piece of bamboo to lift the rostellum and press the
  anther to the stigma; method still used today; not compensated. Smithsonian NMAAHC "Searchable Museum":
  https://www.searchablemuseum.com/edmond-albius-horticulturist/
- Charles Morren (University of Liège) published a hand-pollination method in 1837 but it was too slow to be
  commercial; Richard's claim debunked; thin stick or blade of grass, then thumb; slavery abolished 1848.
  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond_Albius (secondary; consistent with the Linnean piece)
- Vanilla is an orchid genus; flowers receptive to pollination for only six to seven hours; hand pollination with a
  toothpick lifting the rostellum; pods ready about eight to nine months after pollination; curing (sweating, drying,
  conditioning 2 to 6 months); commercial plantations rely on hand pollination because natural rates are low; Albius
  1841. University of Florida IFAS EP656: https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/EP656
- Vanilla is the only edible orchid fruit and the world's second most expensive spice after saffron; hand
  pollination needed outside Mexico; curing takes months. Indian Institute of Spices Research (ICAR):
  https://spices.res.in/products/spices/vanilla.html
notesMd:
- "First" is avoided. The Linnean piece says several people discovered hand pollination independently, and Morren
  did it in 1837 in Belgium. The narration credits Edmond with the quick, practical method farmers adopted, which is
  what all sources agree on, and names the Belgian lab work so no one can say we overclaimed.
- Tool: sources say bamboo, a thin stick, or a blade of grass, so the script says "a thin little stick".
- Pod timing simplified to "about eight months" (IFAS says eight to nine); flower window simplified to "a few
  hours" (IFAS six to seven; Kew is reported as about eight). Curing simplified to "months more".
- Mexico pollinators: older books say only the Melipona bee; the Linnean Society says that was shown wrong
  (Eulaema bees). Narration just says "bees".
- "Why expensive" is given as hand labor plus long growing and curing, which the sources support. We do not quote a
  price because vanilla prices swing hard year to year.
- The often-repeated statue/plaque dates were not verified, so they are left out.

title: Ketchup was fish
transcript: You squeeze ketchup on your fries. Splat. But the very first ketchup had no tomatoes in it. It was made from fish.
So how did a fish sauce turn into the red stuff?
Food historians think it started with Chinese communities in Southeast Asia. They made a salty sauce, and one name for it sounded like kay-tsiap. It meant the brine of pickled fish.
In the sixteen hundreds, British and Dutch sailors tasted it. It kept for months without going bad, which is great on a long boat trip.
Back home, British cooks made their own ketchups out of mushrooms, walnuts, oysters, and anchovies. Still no tomatoes.
Then in eighteen twelve, a doctor in Philadelphia printed a ketchup recipe made with tomatoes. Back then, some people called tomatoes love apples.

And then things got silly. In the eighteen thirties, an Ohio doctor named John Cook Bennett said tomatoes could fix tummy troubles. A pill seller named Archibald Miles jumped in, with Doctor Miles' Compound Extract of Tomato.
The ads made it sound like tomato pills could cure almost anything. The truth? Tests found some tomato pills had no tomato in them at all. Mostly, they just made you poop.
By about eighteen fifty, the pill craze was over. People kept the tomatoes and put them on their food instead.
Fun fact: in Indonesia today, soy sauce is called kecap. Say it out loud. Sound familiar?
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.
sourcesMd:
- Food historian Andrew F. Smith (author of *Pure Ketchup*): "ke-tsiap" meant the brine of pickled fish; probably
  from a Chinese community in northern Vietnam; the word reached English via Indonesia ("kecap") in the late 1600s;
  early British ketchups were made from walnuts, mushrooms and anchovies; "all of the early recipes for ketchup have
  nothing to do with tomatoes". Voice of America Learning English:
  https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/ketchup-an-american-condiment-with-an-asian-connection/3961575.html
- Fish sauce travelled west with Dutch and English sailors in the 1600s and kept for months without spoiling; first
  English recipe in Eliza Smith's *The Compleat Housewife* (1727). Smithsonian Magazine:
  https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/ketchup-fishy-origins-180963511/
- Oysters, mushrooms and walnuts among earlier British ketchup ingredients; Bennett's tomato claims; tomato-pill
  mania through 1850. Hektoen International (medical humanities journal):
  https://hekint.org/2022/07/21/the-tomato-in-medicine-and-the-bloody-mary/
- James Mease, Philadelphia physician, published the first known tomato ketchup recipe in 1812, calling tomatoes
  "love apples". https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mease
- John Cook Bennett: Willoughby Medical College, 1835 first lecture on tomatoes (diarrhea, dyspepsia, indigestion,
  bilious attacks); advised Archibald Miles to rename his "American Hygiene Pill" a tomato extract pill; "Dr. Miles'
  Compound Extract of Tomato"; pills and copycats debuted 1837; by 1840 critics said many contained no tomato; craze
  over by 1850. Mental Floss: https://www.mentalfloss.com/food/when-tomatoes-were-marketed-medicine
- Period primary source: 1838 newspaper item touting Dr. Miles' "concentrated compound extract of Tomatoe" for
  "biliary affections". Camden (S.C.) Commercial Courier, 19 May 1838, via Univ. of South Carolina:
  https://historicnewspapers.sc.edu/lccn/sn92065563/1838-05-19/ed-1/seq-3/ocr
- Kecap = soy sauce (and other fermented sauces) in Indonesian, cognate of "ketchup"; 1690 earliest English record
  "catchup". https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketchup
- Chemist's analysis of Miles' pills (largely aloe, pepper and rhubarb, i.e. laxative-type ingredients) and the 1838
  "Tomato Pill War" with Guy Phelps: reported by Atlas Obscura https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/tomato-pill
notesMd:
- Origin is hedged with "Food historians think". Sources disagree on the exact dialect (Amoy vs Hokkien, which are
  closely related) and place (northern Vietnam vs wider Southeast Asia), so the line stays at "Chinese communities in
  Southeast Asia". Older-than-history claims (300 BC, 7th century China) were found only on weak sites and are left
  out.
- "The very first ketchup had no tomatoes" means the first sauces called ketchup, which every source supports.

  it.

title: When chocolate was money
transcript: You unwrap a chocolate bar. Sweet, smooth, melty. Now imagine chocolate that's bitter, foamy, and spicy, and you drink it.
So how did a spicy drink turn into a candy bar?
People in Mexico and Central America have been drinking cacao for more than three thousand five hundred years. The Olmec drank it. So did the Maya, and later the Aztecs.

You might hear the Aztecs invented chocolate. Not quite. Older peoples drank it long before them. And the oldest cacao traces found so far are in Ecuador, in South America, about five thousand three hundred years old.
They ground roasted beans, mixed them with water, and poured it from cup to cup to make foam, the best part. They added chili, corn, vanilla, or flowers. No sugar, so it was bitter.
Cacao beans were so valuable, the Aztecs used them as money. A price list from fifteen forty-five, in Tlaxcala, Mexico, says a turkey egg cost three beans. A good turkey hen cost one hundred.
Some sneaky sellers even made fake beans. They hollowed them out and stuffed them with sand.

When Europeans first tried it, one traveler said it seemed like a drink for pigs. So they added sugar, and everybody wanted it. Much later, factories made it cheap enough for the chocolate bars you know.
Try this with a grown-up: taste a tiny pinch of plain cocoa powder. Bitter, right? That's closer to the chocolate of long ago.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

  https://www.ancientamericas.org/sites/default/files/06047Powis01.pdf and
  https://sites.bu.edu/gastronomyblog/2017/07/20/cacao-in-olmec-society/

  https://www.worldhistory.org/Chocolate_in_Mesoamerica/

  Cornell University Mann Library exhibit "Chocolate: Food of the Gods":

title: The pineapple you couldn't eat
transcript: Imagine you go to a fancy party, and the star of the table isn't the cake. It's a pineapple. And nobody is allowed to eat it.
So why was a pineapple such a big deal?
Pineapples come from South America. In Britain, two hundred and fifty years ago, it was way too cold to grow them outside.

So rich families built special heated greenhouses just for pineapples, called pineries. Gardeners kept the stoves going, sometimes even sleeping right next to the plants. Each plant took three or four years to make one pineapple.
That made the pineapple the ultimate show-off fruit. A fine one might sit on dinner tables for weeks, just to be admired, and get eaten only once it started to rot. Ew.

Here's a famous story: if you couldn't afford a pineapple, you could rent one for your party, then give it back. A historian who wrote a whole book about pineapples says some sweet shops rented them out by the day. But no one has shown us an old rental receipt yet, so call this one probably true.
And in Scotland, the Earl of Dunmore went all in. In his garden, he built a stone building with a giant stone pineapple on top. It's still standing, and you can even stay the night inside.
So next time you see a pineapple at the grocery store, give it a little bow. It used to be royalty.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

title: The kid, the cold night, and the court case
transcript: You left your juice outside all night. In the morning it's a block of ice with the spoon stuck in it. Gross? Or genius?
So who really invented the popsicle?

Here's the story everybody tells. In nineteen oh five, near San Francisco, an eleven-year-old named Frank Epperson mixed soda powder and water, left it outside with the stirring stick still in it, and went to bed. The night got cold. By morning, the drink had frozen around the stick.
Frank called it the Epsicle. Part Epperson, part icicle.
Now here's what the record shows. Nobody wrote that night down in nineteen oh five. The story shows up years later, when grown-ups were fighting over who owned the idea.
In nineteen twenty-four, Frank got a patent for a frozen treat on a wooden stick. That part is on paper.

Then came the lawsuits. Rival companies said at least ten people had made frozen treats on sticks before him. The popsicle company's lawyer pointed back to nineteen oh five. The National Archives says the popsicle's birth belongs in legends.
Fun fact. Frank's own kids called them Pop's sicles. That's where the name came from.
Try this. Pour juice in a little cup, stand a wooden stick in it, and freeze it overnight. Congratulations. You just acted out the legend.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

title: The carton from Sweden
transcript: You poke the straw in. You squeeze a little too hard. Juice everywhere. Classic.
So where did the juice box come from? Sweden.
In the nineteen forties, a Swedish businessman named Ruben Rausing wanted a cheap paper carton for milk. He gave the job to his lab.
A young lab assistant named Erik Wallenberg went home, thought it over, and came back with a shape made from one piece of paper. A tetrahedron. Four triangle sides, like a little pyramid.

Now, legend versus truth. Ruben's is the famous name. But the shape was Erik's idea, and Erik's name wasn't on the patent. Decades later, in nineteen ninety-one, Swedish engineers gave him a big gold medal for it.
In nineteen fifty-two, the first machine went to a dairy in Lund, Sweden, filling little pyramids with cream.
Pyramids are hard to stack. So in nineteen sixty-three came the brick. Then they learned to fill it germ free, so a box could sit on a shelf without a fridge.
In the early nineteen eighties, those boxes came to America and fit right in a lunchbox. By the end of the decade, about one fifth of all juice sold here came in a box.
Fun fact. In nineteen eighty-nine, food scientists picked germ free packing as their most important idea of the past fifty years.
Today, Wonderade comes in a box too. Eight grams of protein, zero grams of added sugar, and real fruit.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

title: The drink named after a football team
transcript: You just ran around the yard for an hour. You're sweaty, you're thirsty, and your legs feel like wet noodles.
So why did a college football team get its very own drink?
It's nineteen sixty-five at the University of Florida. A Gators coach asks a kidney doctor named Robert Cade a funny question. Why don't football players need to pee after a game?
Cade's team tested the players. In the Florida heat, they were sweating out water and salt, and their blood sugar was low. They were running on empty.
So the doctors mixed water, salt and sugar. By all accounts, the first batch tasted so bad none of the scientists could stomach it. Cade's wife, Mary, suggested lemon juice. That helped.

Now, legend versus truth. The famous story says freshmen drank it during a practice game, then came back in the second half and crushed the older players. Even the university's own write-up calls that part a legend.

Here's what the record shows. In nineteen sixty-six, newspapers noticed the Gators winning in the second half and wrote about the drink. One of Cade's doctors, Jim Free, suggested a name after the team. Gatorade.
Fun fact. The drink has earned the University of Florida more than two hundred fifty million dollars, money that helps pay for research.
Try this. Taste plain water, then water with a squeeze of lemon. Which one would you rather drink after a game?
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

title: The banana in the snack cake
transcript: You unwrap a golden snack cake and bite into the cream. Vanilla. But it didn't start out vanilla.
So what was inside the very first Twinkie?
In nineteen thirty, near Chicago, a bakery manager named James Dewar noticed some machines sitting still. They made strawberry shortcakes, and they only got used when strawberries were in season.

Then came World War Two. Bananas cross the ocean by ship, and the war made shipping hard. The filling switched to vanilla. People liked it, and vanilla stuck.
Now, legend versus truth. Maybe you've heard Twinkies last forever. They don't. In twenty thirteen, the company said they'd stay fresh for forty-five days. Before that, the number was twenty-six.
A reporter at NPR kept one on a shelf for about a year and a half. It didn't fall apart. It turned hard as a rock.
Fun fact. Banana Twinkies came back for a while in the two thousands.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

title: Take the water out
transcript: You tear open a little packet, pour the powder into water, stir, and it turns bright red. Magic.
So why is this drink a powder?
Meet Edwin Perkins. As a kid in Hendley, Nebraska, he worked in his dad's store and was fascinated by a new powder called Jell-O.
When he grew up, in Hastings, Nebraska, he sold a drink syrup called Fruit Smack, in glass bottles. The bottles were heavy, they leaked, and they broke on the way to customers.
So he thought like Jell-O. Take the water out. In nineteen twenty-seven he turned the syrup into powder, packed it in paper envelopes, and called it Kool-Ade.
A packet cost ten cents. When the Great Depression hit, he cut the price to five cents. It sold so well the company moved to Chicago in nineteen thirty-one.

Now, legend versus truth. Why did Kool-Ade, with an e, become Kool-Aid? The story goes that the government said ade was only for drinks made from fruit juice. But nobody has found that rule. Historians just aren't sure.
Fun fact. In nineteen ninety-eight, Nebraska made Kool-Aid its official state soft drink.
Try this. Hold a full bottle of water in one hand and an empty bottle in the other. That difference is the weight Edwin was paying to ship.

title: The cookie 'accident'
transcript: You pull a warm cookie off the tray. The chocolate chips are soft and gooey, but they kept their shape. Somebody planned that. Or did they?
So was the chocolate chip cookie an accident?

In nineteen thirty, Ruth Wakefield and her husband Kenneth bought an old house in Whitman, Massachusetts, and turned it into the Toll House Inn. Ruth had studied cooking in school, and her desserts were famous.
Here's the story everybody tells. One night Ruth ran out of nuts, or out of baker's chocolate, so she chopped up a chocolate bar, expecting it to melt. Surprise. Chocolate chips.
But in the nineteen seventies, Ruth told interviewers a different story. Her guests loved her nut cookie, and she wanted to give them something new. She said chopping the chocolate was on purpose.
So who's right? Nobody can go back and watch. The accident story is fun, and lots of people still tell it. But the one person who was in that kitchen said she meant to do it.
By nineteen thirty-eight, the recipe was in her cookbook, called the Toll House Chocolate Crunch Cookie.
In nineteen thirty-nine, Nestlé agreed to print her recipe on its chocolate. In return, Ruth got free chocolate for life.
Fun fact. In nineteen ninety-seven, a class of third graders helped make the chocolate chip cookie the official state cookie of Massachusetts.
Brought to you by Wonderade, the juice you wish you had when you were growing up.

  accident versions (out of nuts, or out of chocolate) "promote the idea that the invention was an accident"; in the

  chocolate for life per The New York Times.
  https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/12/21/lifestyle/time-delicious-reminder-that-chocolate-chip-cookie-originated-massachusetts

  house in 1930; March 20, 1939 agreement for Nestlé to print the Toll House Cookie recipe on its semi-sweet chocolate

  was a former home economics teacher trying to liven up a butterscotch cookie already sold at the inn.

  bar expecting it to melt): https://lemelson.mit.edu/resources/ruth-wakefield

notesMd:
- The disagreement is presented fairly: the accident story is told first, in full, as "the story everybody tells"
  (it is also told by respected sources like Lemelson-MIT); then Ruth's own 1970s account; then "nobody can go back
  and watch", ending on the fact that the only eyewitness said it was deliberate. We do not call the accident
  tellers liars; the dough-courtroom ends with both sides sharing cookies.
- "Studied cooking in school": LOC says she studied home economics; WBUR says she taught it, Globe says Framingham
  Normal School cooking program. Narration keeps it to "studied".
- Invention year is uncertain (sources say 1930, the 1930s, or 1938), so narration says only "by nineteen
  thirty-eight, the recipe was in her cookbook", which LOC and The Henry Ford support.

  life" is from the Whitman Public Library archive record of the 1939 agreement.

title: Zinc: The Case of the Disappearing Cold
transcript: Princess Punch woke up sniffly, three days before her big game. So Detective Major Orange took the case: can a metal shorten a cold?
The suspect: zinc. Romans made brass with its ore, and medieval India made tons of it. Its disguise today? Pennies, mostly zinc under a copper coat.
Clue one: zinc's day job. About one in ten of your proteins holds zinc, and it helps you grow, heal, taste and smell.
When an egg starts a new life, it even shoots out zinc, filmed as flashes of light. Zinc sparks!
Clue two: young immune cells train at a camp called the thymus, and they need zinc.
Without it? In nineteen sixty-one, Doctor Ananda Prasad described young men in Iran who had stopped growing. Their flatbread diet lacked zinc.
Then, an eyewitness. George Eby's little daughter let a zinc tablet melt in her mouth, and her cold seemed to fade. In nineteen eighty-four, he tested it.

Three later trials gave adults with new colds zinc lozenges or placebos. By day five, seventy percent on zinc had recovered, versus twenty-seven percent on placebo. Colds were about forty percent shorter.
How? Maybe zinc blocks the virus at its doorway into cells. But that's just a theory.
Then, the cross-examination. A twenty twenty-four review called the evidence uncertain. Those trials were adults only, the form and dose mattered, and lozenges can taste bad.
The fine print: never put zinc up your nose. It has taken away people's sense of smell, sometimes for good. Too much zinc pushes out copper. For kids, ask a doctor or pharmacist.
The verdict: case partly closed. Princess Punch rested up, and felt better by game day.
And zinc? Not a magic cure, but an everyday hero you need a little of, from foods like oysters, beef and pumpkin seeds.

  - Prevention: may make little or no difference (low certainty).
